Life from age 4 to 16

I do not have to like getting dirty to like finding out how something works. I am usually quiet in a room until I know what help is needed.

  • family: Lives with her mother and stepmother and spends school holidays with her father; adults cooperate and encourage regular contact.
  • finances: Low income but stable rent and reliable utilities; the household saves slowly for larger expenses.
  • geography: Odessa, Texas.
  • cultureLanguages: English-speaking family with West Texas roots and relatives who differ sharply about music and politics but still share meals.
  • school: Public high school with band instruments available on loan and vocational electives.
  • accessOpportunities: Odessa College outreach, city library events, and school-based workshops are feasible; programs requiring travel or personal equipment are harder.
  • Age 4–5

    Sadie loved listening to her father identify vehicles by engine sound. She liked the guessing game more than riding in the vehicles and preferred arranging toy animals on the dashboard while adults worked.

  • Age 6–7

    She began making up songs with a neighbor and struggled with handwriting that improved through ordinary practice. Her favorite classroom job was handing out supplies because she could notice what people actually needed.

  • Age 8–9

    A family friend showed her basic motorcycle maintenance. She enjoyed understanding the sequence but disliked grease on her hands. Gloves helped, though relatives' jokes about her keeping clean made her reluctant to ask for another lesson.

  • Age 10–11

    She borrowed a clarinet through school and liked playing in a group more than practicing solos. A library craft session introduced paper engineering, and she spent several weekends building pop-up cards for relatives.

  • Age 12–13

    Sadie helped a neighbor run a small resale table and enjoyed polite customer conversations. She was less comfortable bargaining and sometimes accepted a low offer to end an awkward exchange. She also discovered she liked simple electrical diagrams in a vocational unit.

  • Age 14–15

    She stayed in band, took an electronics elective, and repaired a lamp with supervision. A teacher made gloves and cleanup supplies routine, removing a barrier she had considered embarrassing. She still preferred quiet workspaces to the school's busy main shop.

  • Age 16

    Sadie now helps organize band equipment and occasionally assists at resale events. She calls herself untechnical despite successful repairs, partly because she compares herself with relatives who work quickly. She wants to learn at her own pace without having to enjoy dirt or loud machinery.

Life now

  • enjoys: Ensemble clarinet · Paper mechanisms · Clear customer conversations
  • avoids: Grease against bare skin · Pressure bargaining · Crowded noisy shop areas
  • activities: School band · Electronics elective · Occasional resale table
  • demonstratedSkills: Following circuit diagrams · Organizing shared equipment · Precise paper folding
  • unfamiliarActivities: Complex engine repair · Independent sales pricing · Residential programs
  • motivations: Learning without ridicule · Helping a group be ready on time
  • ambitions: Try a supervised repair workshop beyond school · She imagines a stable adult home with music, useful tools, and enough control over her surroundings to work comfortably
  • struggles: Discounts skills that take her longer · Avoids negotiating her own needs
  • supports: Cooperative parents · Band director · Vocational teacher
  • practicalConstraints: Equipment costs · Limited travel funds · Needs practical protective gear

Still uncertain: How will her confidence change with comparison to her own earlier work? · Would she enjoy customer work with training in boundaries and pricing?

Career: Electricians

Preparation: Texas electrician license for non-exempt work.

  • Start with an apprentice license and supervised work.
  • Journeyman: 8,000 supervised hours and exam.
  • Public electrical work runs through a licensed contractor.

Training budget before aid: $2,295 · 1.0 study years in this reference

Still needs funding: $2,295 · loan payments $0/month · included in lifestyle: no

Annual pay before tax: $43,825 · Published paid-training example · apprenticeship

Chosen-life income range: $60,000–$75,000

Budget result: This pay does not cover your lifestyle. Your costs and savings are higher than your take-home pay.

Financial assumptions: A stable home with music, useful tools and control over the work environment is explicit. Small rent and routine expenses are references; protective gear and travel prices are unknown.

Next steps

  • An earlier activity

    I do not have to like getting dirty to like finding out how something works. I am usually quiet in a room until I know what help is needed.

  • Explore electrical work safely

    Visit a public training demonstration or approved student program. Practice algebra, measurement, and reading diagrams. Do not work on live wiring.

  • Compare a paid apprenticeship and college options

    Austin ETA combines four years and 8,000 hours of training. Review admission steps, published pay, tuition, tools, and Texas licensing. Compare technical college classes and construction-management study too.

  • Ask an apprentice and a qualified electrician

    Ask about hours, travel to job sites, physical demands, tuition, and how pay changes with completed training. Ask which pay figures are that employer’s rates and which are area-wide estimates.
